title: Organophosphate Poisoning
subject: Medicine
summary: Organophosphate poisoning is a cholinergic crisis caused by AChE inhibition, presenting with SLUDGE and fasciculations. Rapid recognition, atropine and pralidoxime, and supportive care are essential.

sections.p: Organophosphate poisoning results from exposure to pesticides that irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to excess acetylcholine at synapses.
b: SLUDGE syndrome: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis

t.b: Low plasma AChE confirms exposure; normal values 5–10 U/mL. A value <2 U/mL is diagnostic.
Hypoglycaemia can worsen neurological status; normal 4–8 mmol/L.

sections.p: The WHO organophosphate toxicity scale guides management.
b: Stage 3: severe – seizures, coma, respiratory arrest

t.b: RR >30/min indicates respiratory distress; >40/min is a red flag.
Bradycardia <60/min or tachycardia >120/min signals severe toxicity.

sections.p: In East Africa, the most common sources are agricultural pesticides and household insecticides.

t.b: Ask about recent use of pesticides, accidental ingestion, or occupational exposure.
Check local markets for common OPs; many are sold without regulation.

sections.p: Patients often present with a classic cholinergic picture, but low‑resource settings may miss subtle signs.

t.b: Look for pinpoint pupils, wet mouth, bronchial breath sounds, and fasciculations.
Check for altered mental status; GCS <13 warrants airway support.

sections.p: Limited tests are available; focus on bedside assessment and simple labs.

t.b: Confirms diagnosis; low values support OP poisoning.
Rule out hypoglycaemia; treat if <4 mmol/L.
Assess for respiratory failure; look for hypoxia and hypercapnia.
Identify pulmonary oedema or aspiration; often available in district hospitals.

sections.p: Early recognition of life‑threatening features is vital.

t.b: Any seizure requires benzodiazepines and airway protection.
Bradyarrhythmias or ventricular ectopy need atropine or pacing.

sections.p: Treat the cholinergic crisis with atropine and pralidoxime, plus supportive care.
b: Atropine: antimuscarinic to reverse secretions and bradycardia
Pralidoxime: reactivates AChE if given within 4–6 h
Ventilatory support: intubation if RR <10/min or PaO2 <60 mmHg

t.b: Maintain airway, breathing, circulation; give IV fluids, treat hypoglycaemia.

sections.p: Monitor for delayed neurotoxicity and counsel on safe pesticide use.
b: Repeat AChE after 24 h to assess recovery
Educate on wearing gloves, using protective gear
Advocate for regulation of pesticide sales

t.b: A rise >50% indicates recovery; persistent low levels suggest ongoing exposure.

sections.p: Other causes of cholinergic excess or respiratory distress can mimic OP poisoning.
b: Carbamate poisoning – similar but shorter duration
Acute organophosphate exposure vs. acute asthma

t.b: Carbamate symptoms resolve within 24 h; OP may persist >48 h.
Carbamate patients need less atropine; OP requires higher doses.

sections.p: Certain investigations may give false negatives or positives in low‑resource settings.
b: AChE may be normal if measured late; repeat testing is needed
Glucose may be falsely low if patient is dehydrated

t.b: Test within 24 h of exposure; delayed testing may miss inhibition.
Use point‑of‑care devices; confirm with laboratory if abnormal.

faq.q: What is the first drug to give in OP poisoning?
faq.a: Atropine, to counteract muscarinic effects and improve breathing.
It reactivates acetylcholinesterase if given early, reducing toxin duration.
Yes, severe sympathetic overactivity can raise BP; treat with atropine and supportive care.

exam: What is the most urgent intervention in a patient with OP poisoning and a GCS of 8? — Secure airway, give atropine, consider intubation.
How would you differentiate OP poisoning from severe asthma in a patient with wheeze and bronchorrhoea? — Look for SLUDGE signs, low AChE, and response to atropine.
Why is pralidoxime contraindicated in pregnancy? — It can cross the placenta and cause fetal toxicity.
What is the key laboratory test that confirms OP poisoning? — Plasma acetylcholinesterase activity <2 U/mL.
In a setting without AChE testing, what bedside sign is most reliable for diagnosing OP poisoning? — Pinpoint pupils with excessive salivation and bronchorrhoea.
What is the main reason atropine is avoided in patients with asthma? — It can precipitate bronchospasm.
How does delayed presentation (>6 h) affect the efficacy of pralidoxime? — Oxime binding is less effective after the enzyme has aged.
